blocks.text: Two main groups of proteins participate in the non-specific defence of the body.

Special proteins produced in the liver make the complement system of proteins. This system consists of more than a dozen different proteins that circulate in the blood in an inactive state. When they encounter a microbe, they become active in a sequence. The first protein activates the second and so on. The final five proteins form a membrane-attack complex (MAC) into the plasma membrane of microbe. This complex punctures the plasma membrane of microbe. So, fluids and salts move inside microbe resulting in its swelling and bursting.

blocks.alt: A section of the microbe's membrane (a lipid bilayer) pierced by proteins of the membrane attack complex that line a channel. Arrows of fluid rush from outside, through the channel, down into the cytoplasm of the microbe.
blocks.caption: Figure 21.7: The Complement system of proteins and their functioning (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 21.7).

blocks.text: Interferons are another class of protective proteins that play a key role in body’s defence. They are released by virus-infected cells. They cause nearby cells to enhance their anti-viral defences. Interferons belong to the large class of proteins known as cytokines. These proteins work for communication between cells to trigger the protective defences of the immune system. Interferons also activate other immune cells, such as natural killer cells and macrophages.

blocks.alt: Host cell 1: a virus enters and its nucleic acid makes new viruses, which leave; interferon genes are turned on in the DNA, messenger RNA is made, and interferon molecules are released. They reach host cell 2, where interferon turns on genes for antiviral proteins; the antiviral proteins block viral replication of an arriving virus.
blocks.caption: Figure 21.8: The interferon mechanism to alert other cells (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 21.8).
